We can break the slope formula down into two primary components:

NoteOPTIONAL: Deriving the shortcut formula for variance
To see why this works, write \(\mu = E(X)\) and expand the square inside the expectation. Remember that \(E(X) = \mu\) is a constant, so we can use the properties of expectation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Var(X) &= E\left[(X - \mu)^2\right] \\
&= E\left[X^2 - 2\mu X + \mu^2\right] \\
&= E\left(X^2\right) - 2\mu E(X) + \mu^2 \\
&= E\left(X^2\right) - 2\mu \cdot \mu + \mu^2 \\
&= E\left(X^2\right) - \mu^2
\end{aligned}
\]
In the second line, we expand \((X - \mu)^2\).
In the third line, we use linearity of expectation, and the fact that the expec

NoteOPTIONAL: Proof of \(Var(X+c) = Var(X)\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
Var(X +c) &= E\left(\left(X+c\right)^2\right) - \left(E\left(X+c\right)\right)^2\\
&= E\left(X^2 + 2cX + c^2\right) - \left((E(X))^2 + 2cE(X) + c^2\right) \\
&= E\left(X^2\right) + 2cE(X) + c^2 - \left(E(X)\right)^2 -  2cE(X) - c^2\\
&= E\left(X^2\right) -  \left(E(X)\right)^2 \\
&= Var(X)
\end{aligned}
\]

Important
Continuous random variables differ from discrete random variables in one very important way: If \(X\) is a continuous random variable, we don’t talk about \(P(X = x)\), that is, the probability that \(X\) takes a particular value.
Rather, we ask what is the probability that \(X\) lies in an interval around \(x\). This is because, for continuous random variables, the probabilities are areas under the curve of the probability density function. Tip
Default to a two-sided test.
We want to be rigorous and keep an open mind when we analyze data and evidence. Use a one-sided hypothesis test only if you truly have interest in only one direction.

Tip
Computing a p-value for a two-sided test.
First compute the p-value for one tail of the distribution, then double that value to get the two-sided p-value. That’s it!

Caution
Hypothesis tests should be set up before seeing the data.
After observing data, it is tempting to turn a two-sided test into a one-sided test. Avoid this temptation. Hypotheses should be set up before observing the data.

Also notice: this is one command, spread over two lines. You’ve seen other examples like this but we haven’t said anything about it yet.
When writing code, for readability, you can almost always spread your commands across multiple lines like this. As long as the first line is an “incomplete” command, it will keep reading more lines until it gets a full command. Since planets <- data.frame( kind of leaves R hanging, waiting for more, it will keep going and bring in the next line too, which makes a complete command.
